newsitem.title: USA: UPS strike may raise wage pressures - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UPS strike may raise wage pressures - analysts.

text.p: The United Parcel Service strike could have far-reaching effects on the economy down the road and will be on the agenda when central bank policy-makers meet to set interest rates, analysts said Monday.
About 185,000 UPS workers have been on strike at the nation's largest package carrier since August 4, demanding more full-time positions and benefits for the company's numerous part-time employees.

What has some economists worried is the strike's impact on wages and inflation, and ultimately on interest-rate policy at the Federal Reserve. The central bank's policy-makers are to meet Tuesday, and are widely expected to hold short-term rates steady after raising them in March in a bid to ward off inflation.
Economists said the strike, the biggest since a three-day strike by 400,000 Teamster truckers in 1976, could dampen economic activity in the short term.

"The UPS strike is much more than a fight over low-paying, part-time jobs," said John Challenger, executive vice president of Chicago-based consulting firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas Inc. "It could easily be the most significant economic event of recent years."

The walkout has crippled small package deliveries, and has already cost UPS $650 million in revenues. UPS carried 80 percent of the small packages in the United States before the strike. Its volume has shrunk to about 10 percent of normal.
Retail sales and industrial production in August could be hurt by the strike, which could dampen third-quarter growth, said Mike Penzer, senior economist at Bank of America.

Economists said economic growth would continue in coming months despite the strike. But an agreement favorable to the Teamsters union, which may force UPS to increase wages and the proportion of full-time employees, could lead to similar deals at other companies and thus increase wage pressures across the nation. That, in turn, could spook stock and bond markets.

"(The strike) will reinforce the upward pressure on wages and benefits. These labor compensation demands will show through quickly in higher labor costs," added David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. Inc.

The Fed is keeping a close eye on the strike. Last week, it asked UPS to describe the economic impact of the strike, and its economists were expected to be briefed by company officials before Tuesday's meeting.
"The Fed will be discussing the issue (Tuesday) and will be forced to act on it with a tightening action sometime before the end of the year," Jones said.
But Raymond Worseck, chief economist at AG Edwards & Sons Inc., said the strike was unlikely "by itself, to cause the Fed to raise interest rates."
Bank of America's Penzer said the strike should have little impact on the overall inflation picture.
"We've already embarked on a slow, upward salary trend. This is more of the same," Penzer said. But he added, "The stock market does tend to overreact."
